हंसका: Haṃsakā f.: A mythical cow. Name of one of the four daughters of Surabhi who live in the four directions prote-cting and sustaining them (दिसापाल्यो धार-यन्त्यो दिशः); Haṃsakā sustains the sou-thern direction 5. 100. 7-8; the water of the ocean that was churned by the gods and the demons was mixed with the milk of these four cows and their mother Surabhi 5. 100. 11.
हनूमत्: Hanūmant m.: Name of a monkey-chief. (वानर 3. 146. 59, 74; 3. 147. 2, 5, 6, 22, 24; 3. 149. 4; 3. 150. 1; 3. 264. (9), 10, (12); 3. 266. 32, 60. 63; कपि 3. 146. 72; 3. 147. 17, 20; 3. 149. 5; 3. 270. 13; 7. 80. 29; हरि 3. 148. 4; 3. 150. 3; प्लवं-गम 3. 149. 2; 3. 266. 30). A. Birth: Hanūmant informed Bhīma that he was begotten on the wife of Kesarin by Vāyu 3. 147. 24; hence called ‘son of wind’ वायुसुत 3. 146. 47; वायुतनय 3. 147. 3; वायुपुत्र 3. 275. 60; मारुतात्मज 3. 149. 16; 3. 266 60; 3. 267. 16; 3. 270. 14; 3. 271. 24; अनिलात्मज 3. 264. 23; 3. 266. 36; पवनात्मज 3. 266. 26; 3. 270. 8, 11. B. Description: Having large body (महा-काय 3. 146. 59; महाकपि 3. 147. 17; 7. 80. 29; अतिकाय 3. 146. 71; 3. 270. 14); having long arms (महाबाहु 3. 150. 11; 3. 266. 65); having yellowish eyes (हरि-लोचन 3. 275. 44), or yellowish like wine मधुपिङ्गल 3. 146, 71); of great strength (महाबल 3. 146, 71; 3. 264. 24; महा-वीर्य 3. 147. 13); heroic (शूर 3. 147. 11; वीर्यवन्त् 3. 150. 12); of high spirit (महा-सत्त्व 3. 146. 73); high-souled (महात्मन् 3. 264. 24); endowed with intelligence (बुद्धिमन्त् 3. 264. 10, 24); endowed with intelligence, spirit, and strength (बुद्धि-सत्त्वबलान्वित 3. 147. 11); noble (आर्य 3. 148. 2); praiseworthy for his qualities (गुणश्लाघ्य 3. 147. 11); firm like moun-tain Himavant (हिमवन्तम् इव स्थितम् 3. 264. 10); also 3. 146. 65-71. C. Eminence: Mentioned as chief or excellent among the monkeys: कपीश्वर 3. 148. 1; वानराधिपति 3. 146. 64; वानरवर 3. 146. 71, (7. 80. 9); हरिवर 3. 150. 16; वानरेन्द्र 3. 147. 1, प्लवगेन्द्र 3. 147. 12; वानरपुंगव 3. 146. 59; 3. 147. 11; 3. 150. 11; (3. 266. 24); प्लवगर्षभ 3. 149. 17; (3. 266. 27); कपिशार्दूल 3. 147. 21; 3. 270. 7; (प्लवगसत्तम 3. 266. 52). Meeting with Bhīma: When Bhīma was wandering on the peaks of the Gandhamādana mountain in search of heavenly lotus flowers having heavenly fragrance, he made big noise with his conch near the thicket of banana trees; hear-ing it, the lions and the elephants roared; the big noise aroused Hanūmant who was asleep in the thicket; as he woke up, yawning, he hit the ground with his large tail which looked like the flag staff of Indra and produced sound like a thunder; when Bhīma marched forward to search the source of this sound he saw Hanūmant lying on a thick stone-slab in the midst of the banana trees 3. 146. 59-64; description of Hanūmant 3. 146. 65-71; when Bhīma roared loudly Hanūmant opened his eyes a little, looked despisingly at Bhīma, and asked Bhīma why he woke him up who was happily asleep; he told Bhīma that as an intelligent human being Bhīma should have shown compassion for other beings; Bhīma therefore did not know his धर्म; Hanūmant then asked Bhīma the purpose of his arriving at a place which was not supposed to be visited by human beings; the mountain, beyond that point, could not be crossed unless one had acquired per-fection (सिद्धगति 3. 146. 79); Hanūmant advised Bhīma to eat the roots and fruits to be found there which were as good as अमृत and return 3. 146. 72-81; when Bhīma introduced himself to Hanūmant as a Pāṇ-ḍava and son of Vāyu, Hanūmant responded with a smile but asked Bhīma to return rather than proceed further and meet with danger; when Bhīma insisted that he must proceed and for that purpose Hanūmant should get away from his path, Hanūmant replied that it was not possible for him to move as he was suffering from an ailment; if Bhīma must pro-ceed he should cross over him; when Bhīma said he was prepared to go beyond him and the mountain as Hanūmant had crossed the ocean, Hanūmant asked Bhīma who was that Hanūmant, Bhīma replied that Hanūmant was his brother, meritorious, brave and in-telligent, famous in the Rāmāyaṇa; he crossed the ocean to find out Rāma's wife; knowing Bhīma to be arrogant due to the strength of his arms, Hanūmant again told him that as he could not move due to old age Bhīma should set aside his tail from the path and proceed; Bhīma failed in his attempt to lift the tail and stood with his face turned down due to shame; he bowed down to Hanūmant asking for forgiveness; Bhīma requested Hanūmant to reveal his identity and let him know whether he was a सिद्ध, a god, a Gandharva, or a Guhyaka in the form of a monkey 3. 147. 17-22; Hanūmant then told Bhīma who he really was and that he used to live with Sugrīva on the Ṛśyamūka mountain since the latter was cheated by his brother Vālin 3. 147. 27; Hanūmant further told Bhīma that he had gone out with other crores of monkeys in search of Sītā and was informed by a vulture (Jaṭāyus) about Sītā; he had then jumped over the ocean, one hundred योजनस् wide, seen Sītā in Rāvaṇa's house, and returned after announcing himself to Rāvaṇa; when Rāma finally started (for Ayodhyā) Hanūmant had asked the following boon from Rāma: “May I live as long as the story of Rāma lasts”; the boon was granted to him; Gandharvas and Apsarases sing the narrative of Rāma (तस्य वीरस्य चरितम् 3. 147. 39) to please Hanūmant; Hanūmant again told Bhīma that no mortal could go beyond the point where they met since it was frequented by the gods; Hanūmant informed Bhīma that he had blocked Bhīma's way les the should be attacked or cursed by some one, and that the lake he was searching for was close by 3. 147. 33-41; Bhīma then told Hanūmant that he was highly blessed by his meeting with Hanūmant; Bhīma requested him to show the unrivalled form which he had assumed when he leapt over the ocean; only then Bhīma would believe what Hanūmant had told about him-self; Hanūmant informed Bhīma that it was not possible to assume forms of the bygone age; one acquired the strength, form and prowess according to the युग in which one lived; he had to follow the (rule of the) युग, since no one could go beyond Time (युगे युगे । बल-वर्ष्मप्रभावा हि प्रहीयन्त्य् उद्भवन्ति च … युगं समनुवर्तामि कालो हि दुर-तिक्रमः 3. 148. 7, 8); when Bhīma persisted in his request, Hanūmant increased his body immensely to look like mountain Maināka and showed Bhīma the form he had assumed to cross the ocean 3. 149. 2-4; description of the body 3. 149. 4-7, 13; Hanūmant told Bhīma that he could grow even more, as much as he liked; Bhīma then requested Hanūmant to assume his former shape 3. 149. 8-12 (Hanumant st. 8) when Bhīma asked why Rāma himself had to go to Rā-vaṇa when Hanūmant could destroy Laṅkā, Hanūmant told him that if he had killed Rāvaṇa, Rāma's fame would have suffered 3. 149. 14-20; Hanūmant then permitted Bhīma to depart and showed him the way leading to the Saugandhikavana and the garden of Kubera; he warned Bhima not to pluck the flowers himself and asked him to show regard for the deities; he asked Bhīma not to act rashly but follow the धर्म 3. 149. 21-24; Hanūmant then gave a long discourse on धर्म to Bhīma (explaining to him त्रयी, वार्ता and दण्डनीति; the duties of the four वर्णस्; the conduct of a king) 3. 149. 26-52; Hanūmant contracted his body and embraced Bhīma; the embrace removed Bhīma's fatigue; with faltering voice and tears in his eyes Hanūmant asked Bhīma to remember him and not to tell anyone of his whereabouts; having embraced a mortal (Bhīma) Hanūmant was happy to be reminded of Rāma; Hanūmant offered a boon to Bhīma: if Bhīma so wished Hanūmant could go Hāstinapura and kill the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra or crush their town with a rock 3. 150. 1-9; but Bhīma told Hanū-mant that he (H.) had already done all that he could do for Bhīma; instead of a boon he only asked for Hanūmant's forgiveness and favour; the Paṇḍavas had found in Hanūmant their support which would help them to win the war; hearing that Hanūmant told Bhīma that due to brotherly feelings and friendliness (भ्रातृत्वात् सौहृदाच् चापि 3. 150. 13), whenever Bhīma roared in battles, Hanūmant would add his roar to it and increase its volume; he would stand on the flag-staff of Arjuna and roar which would deprive the enemies of their lives; hence Arjuna's banner often described as marked by a monkey (वानर, कपि, शाखामृग, but the monkey is not named Hanūmant) 5. 47. 46; 5. 59. 13; 6. 56. 7, 9, 20, 27; 6. 67. 3; 6. 78. 9; 6. 112. 114; 7. 9. 14; 7. 17. 21; 7. 80. 8, 9 (the monkey terrified the army of the Kauravas); 7. 80. 29; 7. 102. 6; 7. 114. 81; 9. 9. 59; 10. 12. 25; 14. 51. 54; 14. 82. 29; 14. 83. 12, 23. so saying Hanūmant disappeared 3. 150. 14-15. F. Meeting with Rāma and the fight between Vālin and Sugrīva: When Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa arrived on top of the Ṛśya-mūka mountain and saw five monkeys, Hanūmant, as a messenger of Sugrīva, approached them; Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa first talked with Hanūmant and then approached Sugrīva to form friendship with him 3. 264. 9-11; (later, in the fight between Vālin and Sugrīva) when Rāma could not distinguish between them, Hanūmant stuck a garland round the neck of Sugrīva 3. 264. 33. G. Search for Sītā: After the search for Sītā, when Hanūmant and the other monkey-chiefs were returning to the Ṛśyamūka mountain, on way they rested in the मधुवन; Sugrīva interpreted this behaviour (प्रणय 3. 266. 28) as indicating that Hanūmant and others were successful in their mission; the monkey-chiefs who had gone for the search then approached Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa and Sugrīva 3. 266. 26-30; looking at the complexion of Hanūmant and his gait Rāma understood that he had seen Sītā; Hanūmant informed Rāma that he had brought the good tidings; he then described to Rāma his search for Sītā in the south 3. 266. 31-55 (meeting the female ascetic Prabhāvatī in the house of the Daitya Maya; meeting with Saṃpāti and obtaining from him the information that Sītā must be with Ṛāvaṇa in Laṅkā and that Laṅkā lay beyond the ocean); when no one was prepared to cross the ocean, Hanūmant did it after entering his father (i. e. Vāyu: ततः पितरम् आविश्य पुप्लुवे ऽहं माहार्-णवम्) and killing on way an acquatic Rākṣasī (जलराक्षसी) 3. 266. 57; in Laṅkā, Hanūmant saw Sītā in the inner apartment of Rāvaṇa (तत्र सीता मया दृष्टा रावणान्तःपुरे सती 3. 266. 58); having determined her identity Hanūmant approached her and told her that he was the son of god Wind and the messenger of Rāma; he told Sītā that Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa were safe and had enquired after Sītā's well-being; he assured her that he was a monkey and not a Rakṣasa, and that Rāma would soon arrive in Laṅkā with his monkeys; Sītā told him that she knew him already to be Hanū-mant as was reported to her by the Rākṣasa Avindhya; she gave Hanūmant a jewel and permitted him to leave; to convince Rāma that Hanūmant had met her, Sītā told him the incident of Rāma throwing a reed at a crow on the Citrakūṭa mountain; Hanūmant then burnt Laṅkā and returned to Rāma 3. 266. 58-68. H. Encounter with indi-vidual demons in Rāma's war with Rāvaṇa: Hanūmant marched at the head of the army when it started towards the sea in the south 3. 267. 16; when the demon Dhūmrākṣa attacked the army of the monkeys, Hanū-mant rushed towards him; this act inspired confidence in the monkeys; the fight between the two was fierce like the one between Indra and Prahlāda; Dhūmrākṣa struck Hanūmant with maces (गदा) and clubs (परिघ), and Hanūmant retaliated with trees; finally Hanūmant killed Dhūmrākṣa together with his horses, chariot and charioteer 3. 270. 7, 12-14; when Lakṣmaṇa was engaged in fighting with the demons Vajravega and and Pramāthin, Hanūmant attacked Vajra-vega and killed him with the summit of a mountain (अद्रिशृङ्ग) 3. 271. 24; Hanūmant was among the monkey-chiefs who watched over Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa when they fell down on the ground tied with the arrows of Indrajit 3. 273. 4; he was one of those who applied water, sent by Kubera, to their eyes which enabled them to see invisible beings 3. 273. 10-13; Hanūmant and other monkey-chiefs surrounded Rāvaṇa when he rushed at Rāma 3. 274. 3. I. Sītā's boon: At the time of boon-givings after the war Sītā gave Hanūmant the following boon: “You will live as long as the fame of Rāma lasts (राम-कीर्त्या समं पुत्र जीवितं ते भवीष्यति), and that the heavenly enjoyments will wait on you” 3. 275. 43-44. J. Messenger to Bharata: When Rāma approached the city of Ayodhyā he sent Hanūmant to Bharata as his messenger to give him the good news (of Rāma's return); when Hanūmant, came back, Rāma met Bharata at Nandigrāma 3. 275. 59-60.

Vāyu: ततः पितरम् आविश्य पुप्लुवे ऽहं माहार्-णवम्) and killing on way an acquatic Rākṣasī (जलराक्षसी) 3. 266. 57; in Laṅkā, Hanūmant saw Sītā in the inner apartment of Rāvaṇa (तत्र सीता मया दृष्टा रावणान्तःपुरे सती 3. 266. 58); having determined her identity Hanūmant approached her and told her that he was the son of god Wind and the messenger of Rāma; he told Sītā that Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa were safe and had enquired after Sītā's well-being; he assured her that he was a monkey and not a Rakṣasa, and that Rāma would soon arrive in Laṅkā with his monkeys; Sītā told him that she knew him already to be Hanū-mant as was reported to her by the Rākṣasa Avindhya; she gave Hanūmant a jewel and permitted him to leave; to convince Rāma that Hanūmant had met her, Sītā told him the incident of Rāma throwing a reed at a crow on the Citrakūṭa mountain; Hanūmant then burnt Laṅkā and returned to Rāma 3. 266. 58-68. H. Encounter with indi-vidual demons in Rāma's war with Rāvaṇa: Hanūmant marched at the head of the army when it started towards the sea in the south 3. 267. 16; when the demon Dhūmrākṣa attacked the army of the monkeys, Hanū-mant rushed towards him; this act inspired confidence in the monkeys; the fight between the two was fierce like the one between Indra and Prahlāda; Dhūmrākṣa struck Hanūmant with maces (गदा) and clubs (परिघ), and Hanūmant retaliated with trees; finally Hanūmant killed Dhūmrākṣa together with his horses, chariot and charioteer 3. 270. 7, 12-14; when Lakṣmaṇa was engaged in fighting with the demons Vajravega and and Pramāthin, Hanūmant attacked Vajra-vega and killed him with the summit of a mountain (अद्रिशृङ्ग) 3. 271. 24; Hanūmant was among the monkey-chiefs who watched over Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa when they fell down on the ground tied with the arrows of Indrajit 3. 273. 4; he was one of those who applied water, sent by Kubera, to their eyes which enabled them to see invisible beings 3. 273. 10-13; Hanūmant and other monkey-chiefs surrounded Rāvaṇa when he rushed at Rāma 3. 274. 3. I. Sītā's boon: At the time of boon-givings after the war Sītā gave Hanūmant the following boon: “You will live as long as the fame of Rāma lasts (राम-कीर्त्या समं पुत्र जीवितं ते भवीष्यति), and that the heavenly enjoyments will wait on you” 3. 275. 43-44. J. Messenger to Bharata: When Rāma approached the city of Ayodhyā he sent Hanūmant to Bharata as his messenger to give him the good news (of Rāma's return); when Hanūmant, came back, Rāma met Bharata at Nandigrāma 3. 275. 59-60.
हरि: Hari1 m.: A mythical serpent. Born in the कुल of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, listed by Sūta among those offered in the snake-sacrifice of Janamejaya; described as ‘fast as wind’ (वातवेग) and ‘having excess of poison’ (विषोल्बण) 1. 52. 14, 13.

Hari2 m.: A mythical bird, living in the world of the Suparṇas 5. 99. 13, 1. Born in the कुल of Vainateya (Garuḍa), in the वंश of Kaśyapa; feeding on serpents; marked with श्रीवत्स, his deity is Viṣṇu; by action a Kṣatriya, not obtaining Brahminhood because indulging in the destruction of his kinsmen 5. 99. 2-8.

Hari3 f.: A mythical female being (a female monkey ?) One of the nine daughters (आत्मसं-भवाः) of Krodhavaśā (or of Tāmrā ? 1. 60. 54; in that case क्रोधवशा ‘irascible’); she gave birth to tawney-coloured monkeys (हरयः), to those called वानराः who were energetic ones (तरस्विनः), and the cow-tailed ones (गोलाङ्गूलाः) 1. 60. 58, 62.
हरिक: Harika m.: Name of an ichneumon. Described as ‘looking like the blossom of a reed’ (शरप्रसूनसंकाश 12. 136. 30), mobile, and having red eyes; when the mouse Palita was tasting the piece of flesh, he saw below his deadly enemy, the ichneumon Harika, lying in the crevice of the earth; the ichneumon came out quickly as he got the scent of the mouse, looked up, and licked his mouth for food 12. 136. 30-31; (the mouse also noticed Candraka an owl, his another enemy, up in the nest on the branch of the tree 12. 136. 32); the mouse thus faced danger from the ichneumon and the owl at the same time; he realized that Harika would catch him if he rushed to the ground to save himself from the owl 12. 136. 33, 37; the mouse therefore decided to take refuge with the cat, his third enemy, who was trapped in the net; the mouse pointed out to the cat the danger he was facing owing to the evil intention of the ichneumon and the owl; he offered to cut the threads of the trap in which the cat was caught provided the cat offered him protection from Harika and Candraka 12. 136. 72-73; the cat agreed and when Harika and Candraka saw the mouse confidently resting on the body of the cat, they lost hopes of getting the mouse and returned to their respective homes 12. 136. 82. [See Palita, Lomaśa]
हरिण: Hariṇa m.: A mythical serpent. Born in the कुल of Airāvata, listed by Sūta among those offered in the snake sacrifice of Janamejaya 1. 52. 10, 1.
हरिद्रक: Haridraka m.: A mythical serpent. Son of Kadrū, listed among her sons by Sūta at the request of Śaunaka 1. 31. 12, 2.
हलिक: Halika m.: A mythical serpent. Son of Kadrū, listed among her sons by Sūta at the request of Śaunaka 1. 31. 15, 2.
हलीसक: Halīsaka m.: A mythical serpent. Born in the कुल of Vāsuki, listed by Sūta among those offered in the snake sacrifice of Janamejaya; some of the serpents in this family were dark-red, some white; all were ferocious, huge and having excess of poison (विषोल्बण) 1. 52. 5, 4.
हस्तिपद: Hastipada m.: A mythical serpent. Son of Kadrū, listed among her sons by Sūta at the request of Śaunaka 1. 31. 9, 2.
हस्तिभद्र: Hastibhadra m.: A mythical serpent, living in Bhogavatī Purī 5. 101. 13, 1. Son of Surasā and Kaśyapa 5. 101. 4, 17; description 5. 101. 4-7; also listed by Sūta among the sons of Kadrū 1. 31. 14, 2.
हिरण्यवाह: Hiraṇyavāha m.: A mythical serpent. Born in the कुल of Vāsuki, listed by Sūta among those offered in ths snake sacrifice of Janamejaya; some serpents from this family were dark-red, others white; all of them were ferocious, huge and having excess of poison (विषोल्बण) 1. 52. 6, 4.
हेमगुह: Hemaguha m.: A mythical serpent. Son of Kadrū, listed among her sons by Sūta at the request of Śaunaka 1. 31. 9, 2.
हेमवर्ण: Hemavarṇa m.: A mythical bird, living in the world of the Suparṇas 5. 99. 14, 1. Born in the कुल of Vainateya (Garuḍa), in the वंश of Kaśyapa; feeding on serpents; marked with श्रीवत्स, his deity is Viṣṇu; by action a Kṣatriya, not obtaining Brahmin-hood because indulging in destroying his kinsmen 5. 99. 2-8.
ह्राद: Hrāda m.: A mythical serpent. He was one of those snakes who received the white snake issuing from the mouth of Balarāma and entering the ocean 16. 5. 15, 12,
हंसकाकीय: Haṃsakākīya nt.: Name of an आख्यान 1. 2. 170. Listed in the contents of the Karṇaparvan where it occurs as a part of the harsh dialogue which took place between Karṇa and Śalya when they started out for war; the dialogue was full of abuse (प्रयाणे परुषश् चात्र संवादः कर्णशल्ययोः । हंसकाकीयम् आख्यानम् अत्रैवाक्षे-पसंहितम्) 1. 2. 170; related to the अध्याय 8. 28.
हयशिरस्: Hayaśiras nt.: Name of an आख्यान (forming part of the Nārāyaṇīya) 12. 335. 72; it occurs in stanzas 12. 335. 3-70. A. Description: Described as a Purāṇa equal in importance to the Veda (पुराणं वेदसंमितम्) 12. 335. 7; (पुराणम् वेदसंमितम्) 12. 335. 72; (पौराणम् एतद् आख्यातम् रूपं वरदम् ऐश्वरम् 12. 335. 69). B. Narration: It was originally narrated by Vyāsa to king Yudhiṣṭhira (12. 335. 7), at the latter's request (12. 335. 8-9), and next by Vaiśaṃ-pāyana to Janamejaya 12. 335. 6-7, 72. C. Contents: The आख्यान narrates how Hari-Nārāyaṇa (12. 335. 21, 23, 33, 53, 62-63, 67-69), also called Madhusūdana (12. 335. 64), Viśveśa (12. 335. 49), Īśāna (12. 335. 28), Bhagavant Puruṣa (12. 335. 43, 56), Puruṣottama 10. 335. 62, 65, Puruṣa (12. 335. 56), Śveta Puruṣa (12. 335. 60), and Prabhu 12. 335. 44, 49, 56 (आदिकरं प्रभुम्), assumed the form of a horse's head (हयशिरस्) to retrieve the Vedas which were forcibly taken away by the demons Madhu and Kaiṭabha from Brahman 12. 335. 21-69. D. फलश्रुति: The studies of a Brāhmaṇa who listens or commits to memory this आख्यान are never lost to him 12. 335. 70 (यो ह्य् एतद् ब्राह्मणो नित्यं शृणुयाद् धारयेत वा । न तस्याध्ययनं नाशम् उपगच्छेत् कदाचन ॥ ).
हरणहारिक: Haraṇahārika nt.: Name of the 18th पर्वन् in the list of a hundred sub-पर्वन्स् of the Bhārata supposed to have been made by Vyāsa in the Parvasaṃgraha 1. 2. 38, 33, 70. The title is explained by Nīla. on Bom. Ed. 1. 2. 46. as: हरणं दायः पारिबर्हम् इति यावत् । तस्य हारिका समानयनम्; it occurs after the Subhadrāharaṇaparvan 1. 2. 38; referred to while listing the contents of the Ādiparvan as “where Kṛṣṇa brought with him nuptial gifts (for the Pāṇḍavas)” (हरणं गृह्य सं-प्राप्ते कृष्णे देवकिनन्दने) 1. 2. 93; related to the अध्याय 1. 213. (Nī. on Bom. Ed. 1. 2. 126 cites the following stanza: मानघ्नस्यापि जामातुर् मानं संवर्धयेद् बुधः । स्वसुर् हर्त्रे ऽर्जुनायापि ददुर् वित्तानि वृष्णयः ॥ )
हरिगीता: Harigītā f. (pl.): Name of the tract (?) 12. 336. 49. The धर्म to be practised by the Vratins was once told, with all the injun-ctions to be observed (?), by Vaiśaṃpāyana to Janamejaya in the Harigītās (व्रतिनां चापि यो धर्मः स ते पूर्वं नृपोत्तम । कथितो हरिगीतासु समासविधिकल्पितः) 12. 336. 49; this dharma, together with its secrets and complete collection, was obtained by Nārada from Nārāyaṇa himself (नारदेन तु संप्राप्तः सरहस्यः ससंग्रहः । एष धर्मो जगन्नाथात् साक्षान् नारायणान् नृप) 12. 336. 50.
हरिवंश: Harivaṃśa m.: Name of the 99th पर्वन् in the list of a hundred sub-पर्वन्स् of the Bhārata supposed to have been made by Vyāsa in the Parvasaṃgraha 1. 2. 69, 33, 70. Also called पुराण 1. 2. 69; it is known as an appendix (खिलसंज्ञित) 1. 2. 69, and hence is counted among the खिलस् (खिलेषु … प्रकीर्तितम्) which are mentioned at the end of the eighteen major पर्वन्स् of the Bhārata 1. 2. 233.
हैडिम्ब: Haiḍimba nt.: Name of the 9th पर्वन् in the list of a hundred sub-पर्वन्स् of the Bhārata supposed to have been made by Vyāsa in the Parvasaṃgraha 1. 2. 35, 33, 70. The contents of the पर्वन् are alluded to as: here are narrated the meeting of the Pāṇḍavas with Hiḍimbā in the forest and the birth of Ghaṭotkaca 1. 2. 84; the incident is referred to in Vaiśaṃpāyana's summary of the events made for Janamejaya (where angered Bhīma killed Hiḍimba in the terrifying forest) 1. 55. 19; the पर्वन् is related to the अध्यायस् 1. 139-142 (the birth of Ghaṭotkaca is actually narrated in the first अध्याय of the next sub-पर्वन् entitled Bakavadhaparvan 1. 143. 27-34).
ह्रदप्रवेशन: Hradapraveśana nt.: Name of the 75th पर्वन् in the list of a hundred sub-पर्वन्स् of the Bhārata supposed to have been made by Vyāsa in the Parvasaṃgraha 1. 2. 59, 33, 70. The incidents of this sub-पर्वन्स् are referred to in Dhṛtāṣṭra's summary of the events made for Saṃjaya 1. 1. 149-150 (Saubala (Śakuni), the cause of the game of dice which led to disharmony, was killed by Sahadeva; then the tired Duryodhana, who had lost his chariot, went to a pond and having blocked its water rested there); the पर्वन् is related to the अध्यायस् 9. 17-28.
हस्त: Hasta m.: Name of a constellation, also called Sāvitra (1. 125. 30). A. Description: Consisting of five stars (पञ्चतार) 1. 125. 30. B. Religious rites: (1) दान: Nārada told Devakī (13. 63. 2-4) that by observing fast and giving a gift under the Hasta constellation of a chariot to which four elephants were yoked, one obtained the highest worlds where all pious wishes were fulfilled (हस्ते हस्तिरथं दत्त्वा चतुर्युक्तम् उपोषितः । प्राप्नोति परमा̆ल् लोकान् पुण्यकामसमन्वितान्) 13. 63. 16; (2) Yama told Śaśabindu (13. 89. 1) that by offering a काम्य श्राद्ध under Hasta one obtained the desired fruit (हस्तेन फलभाग् भवेत्) 13. 89. 6 (Nī. on Bom. Ed. 13. 89. 6: फलभाक् इष्टार्थभाक्). C. Simile: Droṇa standing in the arena with the five Pāṇḍava brothers appeared like the Moon in conjunction with the constella-tion Sāvitra (Hasta) consisting of five stars (पञ्चतारेण संयुक्तः सावित्रेणेव चन्द्-रमाः) 1. 125. 30 (Nī. on Bom. Ed. 1. 135. 30: सावित्रेण हस्तनक्षत्रेण).
हंसकूट: Haṃsakūṭa m.: Name of a mountain. When Pāṇḍu, with his two wives, left for forest (1. 110. 37, 42), he reached Gandha-mādana, from where he crossed Haṃsakūṭa to reach Śataśṛṅga where he became an ascetic 1. 110. 43. 45.
हंसप्रपतन: Haṃsaprapatana nt.: Name of a तीर्थ। On the river Gaṅgā (गङ्गायाम्); famous in the three worlds (त्रैलोक्यविश्रुत) 3. 83. 82.
हरिगिरि: Harigiri m.: Name of a mountain. One of the six mountains of the Kuśa-dvīpa; all the six mountains are said to be best among the mountains (पर्वतोत्तमाः); the distance between them doubles as one proceeds from the one to the other (तेषाम् अन्तरविष्कम्भो द्विगुणः प्रविभागशः) 6. 13. 11.
हरिस्रावा: Harisrāvā f.: Name of a river. Listed by Saṃjaya among the rivers of the Bhāratavarṣa; people used its water for drinking 6. 10. 27, 13; described as a big river (महापगा) 6. 10. 27 (or Mahāpagā name of an independent river ?); all the rivers listed by Saṃjaya are said to be mothers of the universe and very strong 6. 10. 35 (for citation see Atikṛṣṇā).
हस्तिसोमा: Hastisomā f.: Name of a river. Listed by Saṃjaya among the rivers of the Bhāratavarṣa; people used its water for drinking 6. 10. 18, 13 (for other details see Harisrāvā).
हिडिम्बवन: Hiḍimbavana nt.: Name of a forest. Described as a large forest (महारण्य) 3. 13. 85; Pāṇḍavas approached it and slept there; there they met Hiḍimbā and Hiḍimba and Bhīma killed the latter in an encounter 3. 13. 86-97.
हिमवत्: Himavant m.: Name of a mountain; also referred to as Haimavata 1. 116. 27; Haimavata giri 9. 37. 26; Haima 13. 20. 28; Himadri 8. 13. 16, 20; Himālaya 6. 32. 25; Tuṣāragiri 13. 14. 109; Śvetanaga 8. 13. 20. A. Location: In the north (अत्र (i. e. उत्तरस्यां दिशि) वै हिमवत्पृष्ठे 5. 109. 5; ततो ऽगच्छत् स भगवान् उत्तराम् उत्त-मां दिशम् । हिमवन्तं गिरिश्रेष्ठम्) 13. 20. 2; 13. 19. 14, 16; 13. 20. 28; 1. 189. 22; 5. 14. 5; ततस् ते नियतात्मान उदीचीं दिशम् आश्रिताः । ददृशुर् … हिमवन्तम्) 17. 2. 1; Arjuna went to the north to reach the top of Himavant (जगाम … दिशं ह्य् उदीचीं कौरव्यो हिमवच्छिखरं प्रति) 3. 39. 11; प्रायाद् उदङ्मुखः । शैशिरं गिरिम् उद्दिश्य) 12. 314. 2 (Nī. on Bom. Ed. 12. 327. 2: शैशिरं गिरिं हिमालयम्); the world to the north of Himavant is called Vara (उत्तरे हिम्वत्पार्श्वे … स वरो लोक उच्यते) 12. 185. 8; Meru is to the north of Himavant (मेरुं पर्वतम् … हिमवत्-पार्श्व उत्तरे) 14. 4. 25; lies at a long dis-tance (प्रकृष्टे चाध्वनि हिमवान्) 3. 191. 4; 2. 23. 4, 9; 2. 24. 1; the mountain of sun-rise lies at the extreme end of Himavant (ये परार्धे हिमवतः सूर्यदयगिरौ नृपाः) 2. 48. 8; in the west, the root of Himavant reaches up to Mandara and its end cannot be reached even after a thousand years (अत्र (i. e. in the west 5. 108. 2) मूलं हिमवतो मन्दरं याति शाश्वतम् । अपि वर्षसह-स्रेण न चास्यान्तो ऽधिगम्यते) 5. 108. 9; the slope of Himavant is to the north of the Kosalas 2. 27. 4; counted by Saṃjaya among the six mountains which stretch towards the east and merge at both ends in the eastern and the western ocean; the dis-tance between these mountains is thousands of योजनस् (प्रागायता महाराज षड् एते … । अवगाढा ह्य् उभयतः समुद्रौ पूर्व-पश्चिमौ । … तेषाम् अन्तरविष्कम्भो योज-नानि सहस्रशः) 6. 7. 2, 4; the gate leading to the lake Mānasa is on the Himavant (not named) (एतद् द्वारं महाराज मानसस्य) 3. 130. 12; the river Sarasvatī rises on Himavant 9. 37. 20; Sarasvatī flows at a distance of a little less than two योजनस् from Kurukṣetra (ऊने द्वियोजने गत्वा … पुण्ये प्रस्थे हिमवतः … अरुणाम् सर-स्वतीं प्राप्य) 9. 4. 48-49; Gaṅgā rises from the golden summit of Himavant (पुरा हिम-वतश् चैषा हेमशृङ्गाद् विनिःसृता) 1. 158. 17; at the foot of Himavant flows the river Mālinī (प्रस्थे हिमवतो रम्ये मालिनीम् अभितो नदीम्) 1. 66. 8; the Bāhlīkas lie outside the range of the Himavant (बहिष्कृता हिमवता … तान् बाह्लीकान् परिवर्जयेत्) 8. 30. 10-11. B. Description: Holy, the holiest of all (पुण्य) 1. 26. 14; 1. 115. 27; 3. 88. 18; 3. 155. 15, 16; 7. 57. 27; 9. 4. 49; 9. 37. 26; 12. 185. 8; 13. 26. 57; 13. 127. 2; (सर्वपुण्यतम) 12. 185. 21; auspicious (शुभ) 3. 175. 6; 9. 4. 49; 12. 185. 21; 12. 320. 8; 13. 10. 5; 13. 126. 33; heavenly (दिव्य) 12. 320. 8; pleasing, very pleasing (रम्य) 1. 66. 8; 1. 106. 8; 9. 43. 9; 13. 127. 3; (सुरम्य) 12. 160. 31; shining (रुचिर) 12. 320. 9; unequalled (अप्रतिम) 12. 320. 8; 13. 127. 11; famous (विख्यात) 13. 26. 57; big mountain (महाशैल) 12. 125. 29; (माहागिरि) 1. 189. 20; 3. 39. 16; 13. 20. 3; 17. 2. 1; (प्रांशु) 9. 50. 32; not accessible, not easily accessible (दुर्ग) 3. 174. 12; F. Epic events: (1) Pāṇḍu left Hāstinapura and lived with his two wives in the forest on the southern side of Himavant giving himself to hunting (अरण्यनित्यः सततं बभूव मृगयापरः ॥ स चरन् दक्षिणं पार्श्वं रम्यं हिमवतो गिरेः) 1. 106. 7-8; (ii) Pāṇḍu crossed Himavant to go to Gandhamādana from where he went to Śataśṛṅga 1. 110. 43; when Pāṇḍu with his two wives wished to go from Śataśṛṅga further north, the ascetics dissuaded him des-cribing to him the higher inaccessible regions of Himavant; they said that the two princesses (Kuntī and Mādrī) would be pained walking on that mountain (गिरेर् अस्य दुर्गान् देशान् बहून् । … गच्छन्त्यौ शैलराजे ऽस्मिन् राज-पुत्र्यौ कथं त्व् इमे । न सीदेतां) 1. 111. 5-10; (3) Vyāsa retired to Hima-vant (हिमवन्तं शिलोच्चयम्) to practise austerities after advising Gāndhārī what she should do about the piece of flesh (मांस-पेशी) born to her 1. 107. 23; (4) Pāṇḍavas grew on Himavant causing wonder to the great sages (हैमवते गिरौ) 1. 115. 27; (5) Arjuna told Aṅgāraparṇa Gandharva that no one had an exclusive claim on Hima-vant (हिमवत्पार्श्वे) (nor on ocean and Gaṅgā) 1. 158. 15; (6) Arjuna, during his exile, went from Gaṅgādvāra to Himavant (हिमवत्पार्श्वम्) 1. 207. 1; (7) Arjuna conquered Himavant, along with Niṣkuṭa, in his expedition to the north before the Rāja-sūya (हिमवन्तं सनिष्कुटम्) 2. 24. 27; (8) Bhīma, in his expedition to the east (2. 26. 1, 7), defeated Jaradgava who ruled over the region near Himavant (हिमवतः पार्श्वे समभ्येत्य जरद्गवम्) 2. 27. 4; (13) Yudhiṣṭhira started from the आश्रम of Nārāyaṇa (3. 155. 1) and reached the tableland of Hima-vant on the seventeenth day (प्रस्थं हिम-वतः पुण्यं ययौ सप्तदशे ऽहनि) 3. 155. 15; from there Gandhamādana could be seen at close quarters (ददृशुः पाण्डवा राजन् गन्धमादनम् अन्तिकात् । पृष्ठे हिमवतः पुण्ये) 3. 155. 16; (14) The Pāṇḍavas lived on the tableland of Himavant (हिमवत्पृष्ठे) eating foods partaken by sages (भुञ्जाना मुनिभोज्यानि), juicy fruits, as also meat of deer killed with purified arrows (शुद्धबाण-हतानां च मृगाणां पिशितान्य् अपि), and different kinds of honey (मधूनि विविधानि च); I. Modes of expression: These are based on various characteristics of the mountain: (a) Stead-iness: (i) Himavant might start moving about, but Duḥśāsana would not rule the earth without Duryodhana (हिमवांश् च परिव्रजेत् । … न चाहं त्वद् ऋते राजन् प्रशासेयं वसुन्धराम्) 3. 238. 31; (ii) If Arjuna's words were to prove false then, indeed, Himavant may move from its place (चलेद् धि हिमवान् स्थानात् … मत्-सत्यं विचलेद् यदि) 2. 68. 35; the same said by Kṛṣṇa (चलेद् धि हिमवाञ् शैलो  … न मे मोघं वचो भवेत्) 5. 80. 48; (b) Solid form: (i) Kṛṣṇa to Draupadī: Himavant may be shattered, but his words would not be false (हिमवाञ् शीर्येत् … न मे मोघं वचो भवेत्) 3. 13. 117; (ii) Duryodhana to Dhṛtarāṣṭra: Even Himavant would be shattered in a hundred thousand ways if hit just once by Duryodhana with his गदा (गदाप्रहाराभिहतो हिमवान् अपि पर्वतः । … विशीर्येत गिरिः शतसहस्रधा) 5. 54. 38; (iii) Hearing Bhīma's loud roar after the death of Jarāsaṃdha people wondered if Himavant had split (किं नु स्विद् धिम-वान् भिन्नः) 2. 22. 9; (c) Not subject to reduction in size: Even Himavant would decay under certain conditions (भक्ष्य-माणो ह्य् अनावापः क्षीयते हिमवान् अपि) 3. 33. 9; (d) Not to be easily toppled down: Himavant is one of the four mountains which cannot be easily toppled down (हिमवान् … चत्वारः पर्वताः केन पातिता भुवि तेजसा) 3. 297. 14; (e) Very large size: Bhīma to Yudhiṣṭhira—Yudhiṣṭhira's wish to hide Pāṇḍavas for a year was like trying to hide Himavant with a handful of grass (तृणानां मुष्टिनैकेन हिमवन्तं तु पर्वतम् । छन्नम् इच्छसि कौन्तेय यो ऽस्मान् सं-वर्तुम् इच्छसि) 3. 36. 22; (f) Strength: Bhīma to Kṛṣṇa—even Himavant, ocean and Indra together cannot rescue a person attack-ed by Bhīma (हिमवांश् च समुद्रश् च वज्री च … । मयाभिपन्नं त्रायेरन् बलम् आस्थाय न त्रयः) 5. 74. 10; (g) Impass-ableness: One cannot say that the back side of Himavant does not exist simply because men have not seen it (यथा हिमवतः पृष्ठं  … न दृष्टपूर्वं मनुजैर् न च तन् नास्ति तावता) 12. 196. 6; (h) Mighty elephants at its foot: Wishing to defeat Yudhiṣṭhira was like driving away with a stick a huge ele-phant in rut roaming at the foot of Himavant with its herd (नागम् … उपत्यकां हैम-वतीं चरन्तम् । दण्डीव यूथाद् अपसे-धसे त्वं यो जेतुम् आशंससि धर्म-राजम् ॥ ) 3. 252. 5. Characteristics: (1) Mytho-logical: (i) Gods assemble on Himavant (विद्यते हि गिरिश्रेष्ठे त्रिदशानां समा-गमः) 3. 40. 30; (ii) Four Lokapālas, gods and sages always come there for the benefit of the world (चत्वारो लोकपालाश् च देवाः सर्षिगणास् तथा । यत्र नित्यं समायान्ति लोकस्य हितकाम्यया) 12. 314. 6; (iii) Kirāta (Śiva) lives on the summit of Hima-vant (हिमवच्छिखरालयः) 3. 40. 29; there is the abode of Rudra on Himavant (रुद्रस्यायतनम्) which is resorted to by Siddhas and Cāraṇas, by Pārṣadas, Piśācas and various forest tribes (वन्यैर् नाना-विधैस् तथा); they all serve Śarva there 13. 19. 16-18; the place is liked by Śiva and he is always present there 13. 19. 19; 5. 109. 5; (iv) Gods, Gandharvas and Apsarases have their playgrounds on many inaccessible regions of Himavant (गिरेर् अस्य दुर्गान् देशान् बहून् … । आक्रीडभूतान् देवानां गन्धर्वाप्सरसां तथा) 1. 111. 6; (v) It has Kubera's gardens (उद्यानानि कुबेर-स्य) 1. 111. 7; (vi) Garutmant, king of birds, always visits it 12. 314. 6; 2. Importance: (i) For Upamanyu, Śiva was like Himavant among mountains (शैलानां हिमवान् गिरिः) 13. 14. 161; (ii) Bhagavān is the Himālaya among those that do not move (स्थावराणां हिमालयः) 6. 32. 25; (iii) Finds mentions in the Daivata-Ṛṣi Vaṃśa 13. 151. 25, 2. F. Epic events: (1) Pāṇḍu left Hāstinapura and lived with his two wives in the forest on the southern side of Himavant giving himself to hunting (अरण्यनित्यः सततं बभूव मृगयापरः ॥ स चरन् दक्षिणं पार्श्वं रम्यं हिमवतो गिरेः) 1. 106. 7-8; (ii) Pāṇḍu crossed Himavant to go to Gandhamādana from where he went to Śataśṛṅga 1. 110. 43; when Pāṇḍu with his two wives wished to go from Śataśṛṅga further north, the ascetics dissuaded him des-cribing to him the higher inaccessible regions of Himavant; they said that the two princesses (Kuntī and Mādrī) would be pained walking on that mountain (गिरेर् अस्य दुर्गान् देशान् बहून् । … गच्छन्त्यौ शैलराजे ऽस्मिन् राज-पुत्र्यौ कथं त्व् इमे । न सीदेतां) 1. 111. 5-10; (3) Vyāsa retired to Hima-vant (हिमवन्तं शिलोच्चयम्) to practise austerities after advising Gāndhārī what she should do about the piece of flesh (मांस-पेशी) born to her 1. 107. 23; (4) Pāṇḍavas grew on Himavant causing wonder to the great sages (हैमवते गिरौ) 1. 115. 27; (5) Arjuna told Aṅgāraparṇa Gandharva that no one had an exclusive claim on Hima-vant (हिमवत्पार्श्वे) (nor on ocean and Gaṅgā) 1. 158. 15; (6) Arjuna, during his exile, went from Gaṅgādvāra to Himavant (हिमवत्पार्श्वम्) 1. 207. 1; (7) Arjuna conquered Himavant, along with Niṣkuṭa, in his expedition to the north before the Rāja-sūya (हिमवन्तं सनिष्कुटम्) 2. 24. 27; (8) Bhīma, in his expedition to the east (2. 26. 1, 7), defeated Jaradgava who ruled over the region near Himavant (हिमवतः पार्श्वे समभ्येत्य जरद्गवम्) 2. 27. 4; (9) Yudhiṣṭhira in his childhood was instru-cted by Merusāvarṇīn on Himavant (हिम-वत्य् अनुशिष्टो ऽसि मेरुसावर्णिना पुरा) 2. 69. 12; (10) Lomaśa showed the gate of the Mānasa lake to Yudhiṣṭhira (एतद् द्वारं महाराज मानसस्य प्रकाशते । वर्षम् अस्य गिरेर् मध्ये) 3. 130. 12; (11) Arjuna went to the summit of Himavant to practise austerities in order to meet Indra and Śiva (हिमवच्छिखरं प्रति । … शुशुभे हिमवत्पृष्ठे । … हिमवत्पृष्ठम् आश्रितः । ) 3. 39. 10-12, 16, 26; (12) From Subāhu's realm the Pāṇḍavas proceeded to Himavant to meet Arjuna (हिमवन्तम् गिरिं प्रति) 3. 141. 27; (13) Yudhiṣṭhira started from the आश्रम of Nārāyaṇa (3. 155. 1) and reached the tableland of Hima-vant on the seventeenth day (प्रस्थं हिम-वतः पुण्यं ययौ सप्तदशे ऽहनि) 3. 155. 15; from there Gandhamādana could be seen at close quarters (ददृशुः पाण्डवा राजन् गन्धमादनम् अन्तिकात् । पृष्ठे हिमवतः पुण्ये) 3. 155. 16; (14) The Pāṇḍavas lived on the tableland of Himavant (हिमवत्पृष्ठे) eating foods partaken by sages (भुञ्जाना मुनिभोज्यानि), juicy fruits, as also meat of deer killed with purified arrows (शुद्धबाण-हतानां च मृगाणां पिशितान्य् अपि), and different kinds of honey (मधूनि विविधानि च); here they completed the fifth year of their forest life 3. 157. 7-9; (15) On their return journey the Pāṇḍavas crossed the inaccessible regions of Himavant (दुर्गं हिमवत्-प्रदेशम्) to reach once again the realm of Subāhu 3. 174. 12; (16) When the Pāṇḍa-vas lived in Dvaitavana on the bank of Sarasvatī (सरस्वतीम् एत्य निवासकामाः) 3. 174. 21, Bhīma noticed the regions of Himavant (देशान् गिरेर् हिमवतः) 3. 175. 6; (17) Arjuna told Uttarā that he was born on the plateau of Himavant (जातो हिमवत्पृष्ठे) 4. 39. 14; (iii) King Avikṣit and (iv) Vibhīṣaṇa (हिमवान् इव सुस्थिरः) 14. 4. 20; 3. 270. 2; (v) Hanūmant (हिमवन्तम् इव स्थितम्) 3. 264. 10; (vi) Yudhiṣṭhira advised to be steady like Himavant (स्थिरो भव यथा राजन् हिमवान्) 12. 126. 51; (b) Immovability: (i) Kṣemavṛddhi under the attack of arrows (तद्बाणवर्षं … विषेहे … हिमवान् इव निश्चलः) 3. 17. 13; (ii) Duryodhana (नाचलद् गिरिराड् इव) 6. 74. 7; (c) Firmness: Arjuna (धैर्येण हिमवान् इव) 1. 179. 9; (d) Undisturbed nature: A learned man (पण्डितः … स्थितः प्रकृत्या हिमवान् इवाचलः) 12. 219. 15; (e) Unconquerable: Arjuna (दुर्धर्षो हिमवान् इवाचलः) 14. 77. 1; (f) Trust-worthy: A king (विश्वास्यो हिमवान् इव) 12. 57. 29; (g) Store of jewels: The Bhārata text (यथा समुद्रः … यथा च हिमवान् गिरिः । ख्याताव् उभौ रत्ननिधी तथा भारतम् उच्यते) 18. 5. 52; (h) Vastness, extensive-ness: King Sumitra (हिमवान् वा महाशैलः समुद्रो वा महोदधिः । महत्वान् नान्व-पद्येताम् रोदस्योर् अन्तरं यथा) 12. 125. 29; (i) Greatness, largeness: Dadhīca (अतिकायः स तेजस्वी … जज्ञे शैलगुरुः प्रांशुः) 9. 50. 32; (j) Superiority: Arjuna (हिमवान् इव शैलानाम् … वरः) 4. 2. 19-20; Bhīṣma to Arjuna (unexpressed simile) (गिरीणां हिमवान् वरः … श्रेष्ठस् त्वम् असि धन्विनाम्) 6. 116. 33; (k) Not to be toppled down: Himavant, one of the four mountains with which the four Pāṇḍavas are compared (हिमवान् पारियात्रश् च विन्ध्यो मलय एव च । चत्वारः पर्वताः केन पातिता भुवि तेजसा) 3. 297. 14; (2) Com-parison with Himavant under certain situa-tions: (a) Arjuna with the great monkey on his banner shone like Himavant with fire (हिमवान् इव वह्निना) 7. 80. 29; (b) (i) Karṇa said he would withstand Arjuna in battle as does Himavant the fierce, stormy wind (प्रभञ्जनं मातरि-श्वानम् उग्रम् । … हिमवान् इवाचलः) 8. 29. 15; (ii) Similarly Alambusa checked the attack of Arjuna (प्रभञ्जनम् इवाद्रि-राट्) 7. 142. 37; (iii) Ghaṭotkaca's son (Añjanaparvan) withstood the attack of Aśvatthāman (प्रभञ्जनम् इवाद्रिराट्) 7. 131. 44; (c) (i) The Saṃśaptakas showered weapons on Arjuna from all sides as the clouds, hurled by winds, rush at Himavant in the rainy season (मरुद्भिः प्रेषिता हिमवन्तम् इवोष्णगे) 8. 14. 8 (Nī. on Bom. Ed. 8. 19. 8; उष्णगे ग्रीष्मे गते सति प्रावृषीत्य् अर्थः । उष्णो ग्रीष्मो गतो ऽतीतो यत्र स उष्णगः कालविशेष इति विग्रहः); (ii) Similarly Vaitahavyas attacked Pratar-dana (हिमवन्तम् इवाम्बुदाः) 13. 31. 38; (d) Duryodhana who had put on a head-gear and wore a golden armour shone like the golden king of mountains (काञ्चनः शैलराड् इव) 9. 54. 15; (e) When blood began to flow down from the body of Vajradatta's elephant, hit by the arrows of Arjuna, he was compared with Himavant with many streams (हिमवान् इव शैलेन्द्रो बहुप्रस्रवणस् तदा) 14. 74. 20; (f) (i) Bāhlīka, with his head cut off, fell down like Himavant when hit by वज्र (वज्राहत इवाद्रिराट्) 7. 132. 15; (ii) Daṇḍa's elephant in similar condition (हिमाद्रिकूटः कुलिसाहतो यथा) 8. 13. 20; (3) Summit of Himavant as an उपमान: (a) Daṇḍa's elephant, white like snow and wearing golden garlands, was the image of the summit of Himavant (हिमावदातेन सुवर्णमालिना हिमाद्रिकूटप्रतिमेन दन्-तिना) 8. 13. 16; (द्विपं श्वेतनगाग्रसं-निभम्) 8. 13. 20; (b) Hump on Śiva's bull compared with the summit of the snowy mountain (तुषारगिरिकूटाभम्) 13. 14. 109; (c) The residences, tall and studded with minerals, looked like summit of Himavant (बहुधातुपिनद्धाङ्गान् हिमवच्छिखरान् इव) 2. 31. 23; 1. 176. 22; (d) Duryodhana's गदा had the form of the summit of Hima-vant (हिमवच्छिखराकाराम्) 9. 32. 47; (4) Earth has Himavant as her crest (शैल-राजावतंशकाम्) 1. 69. 27; (5) Certain animals, birds and other objects from Hima-vant serve as उपमानस्: (a) Elephants (i) Arjuna and Karṇa fought as do two elephants in rut from Himavant (यथा गजौ हैम-वतौ प्रभिन्नौ) 8. 65. 2; (ii) kings assembled for Draupadī's स्वयंवर (यथा हैमवता गजेन्द्राः) 1. 178. 2; (iii) Heroes defeated by Arjuna slept like grown up elephants from Himavant (नागा यथा हैम-वताः प्रवृद्धाः) 4. 49. 15; (iv) (a) Elephants from Himavant as उपमेय: The elephants from Himavant with golden nets hanging from their bodies looked like clouds with lightnings (सुकल्पिता हैमवताः … सुवर्णजालावतता बभुर् गजा तथा यथा वै जलदाः सविद्युतः) 8. 62. 36; (b) Lions: (i) Kuntī blessed Karṇa saying that when he became a young man he would be like a lion with a mane from the forest of Himavant (हिमवद्वनसंभूतं सिंहं केसरिणं यथा) 3. 292. 21; (ii) Bhīma rushed at Duḥśāsana as a lion from Hima-vant rushes at a jackal (सिंहो यथा हैम-वतः शृगालम्) 2. 68. 15; (iii) Bhīma, Arjuna and Kṛṣṇa went to Jarāsandha's residence as do the Himavant lions to a cow-pen (गोवासम् इव … सिंहा हैमवता यथा) 2. 19. 25; (c) Swans: (i) Horses adorned with चामरस्, running on the battle-field looked like swans from the summit of Himavant touching the earth (हंसा हिम-वतः प्रस्थे पिबन्त इव मेदिनीम्) 9. 8. 12; (ii) Thousands of horses hit by Arjuna's arrows fell down like swans falling down on the slopes of Himavant when struck by water (हंसा हिमवतः पृष्ठे वारिविप्र-हता इव) 7. 66. 19; (d) Kiṃśuka tree: Bhīma and Duryodhana, wounded and smear-ed with blood, looked like two Kiṃśuka trees in blossom on Himavant (हिमवति पुष्पिताव् इव किंशुकौ) 9. 57. 31; (e) A leaf: Indra, humiliated, trembled as does a leaf of a fig tree, stirred by wind, on the Himavant summit (अनिलेनेव नुन्नम् अश्वत्थपत्रं गिरिराजमूर्ध्नि) 1. 189. 22; (f) A cave: A king is said to be like a cavern on Hima-vant, inaccessible and difficult to enter (दुरा-सदां दुष्प्रवेशां गुहां हैमवतीम् इव) 12. 83. 39. (6) Vyāsa surrounded by his pupils and his son at the foot of Himavant looked like the lord of the Bhūtas (Śiva) sur-rounded by Bhūtas (शुशुभे हिमवत्पादे भूतैर् भूतपतिर् यथा) 12. 337. 12; (7) Himavant an उपमेय: Himavant without the sound of the recitation of the Vedas did not shine like moon when covered with dust and darkness at the time of the eclipse or like a habitation of the Niṣādas (ब्रह्मघो-षैर् विरहितः पर्वतो ऽयं न शोभते । रजसा तमसा चैव सोमः सोपप्लवो यथा ॥ न भ्राजते यथापूर्वं निषादा-नाम् इवालयः) 12. 315. 13-14. I. Modes of expression: These are based on various characteristics of the mountain: (a) Stead-iness: (i) Himavant might start moving about, but Duḥśāsana would not rule the earth without Duryodhana (हिमवांश् च परिव्रजेत् । … न चाहं त्वद् ऋते राजन् प्रशासेयं वसुन्धराम्) 3. 238. 31; (ii) If Arjuna's words were to prove false then, indeed, Himavant may move from its place (चलेद् धि हिमवान् स्थानात् … मत्-सत्यं विचलेद् यदि) 2. 68. 35; the same said by Kṛṣṇa (चलेद् धि हिमवाञ् शैलो  … न मे मोघं वचो भवेत्) 5. 80. 48; (b) Solid form: (i) Kṛṣṇa to Draupadī: Himavant may be shattered, but his words would not be false (हिमवाञ् शीर्येत् … न मे मोघं वचो भवेत्) 3. 13. 117; (ii) Duryodhana to Dhṛtarāṣṭra: Even Himavant would be shattered in a hundred thousand ways if hit just once by Duryodhana with his गदा (गदाप्रहाराभिहतो हिमवान् अपि पर्वतः । … विशीर्येत गिरिः शतसहस्रधा) 5. 54. 38; (iii) Hearing Bhīma's loud roar after the death of Jarāsaṃdha people wondered if Himavant had split (किं नु स्विद् धिम-वान् भिन्नः) 2. 22. 9; (c) Not subject to reduction in size: Even Himavant would decay under certain conditions (भक्ष्य-माणो ह्य् अनावापः क्षीयते हिमवान् अपि) 3. 33. 9; (d) Not to be easily toppled down: Himavant is one of the four mountains which cannot be easily toppled down (हिमवान् … चत्वारः पर्वताः केन पातिता भुवि तेजसा) 3. 297. 14; (e) Very large size: Bhīma to Yudhiṣṭhira—Yudhiṣṭhira's wish to hide Pāṇḍavas for a year was like trying to hide Himavant with a handful of grass (तृणानां मुष्टिनैकेन हिमवन्तं तु पर्वतम् । छन्नम् इच्छसि कौन्तेय यो ऽस्मान् सं-वर्तुम् इच्छसि) 3. 36. 22; (f) Strength: Bhīma to Kṛṣṇa—even Himavant, ocean and Indra together cannot rescue a person attack-ed by Bhīma (हिमवांश् च समुद्रश् च वज्री च … । मयाभिपन्नं त्रायेरन् बलम् आस्थाय न त्रयः) 5. 74. 10; (g) Impass-ableness: One cannot say that the back side of Himavant does not exist simply because men have not seen it (यथा हिमवतः पृष्ठं  … न दृष्टपूर्वं मनुजैर् न च तन् नास्ति तावता) 12. 196. 6; (h) Mighty elephants at its foot: Wishing to defeat Yudhiṣṭhira was like driving away with a stick a huge ele-phant in rut roaming at the foot of Himavant with its herd (नागम् … उपत्यकां हैम-वतीं चरन्तम् । दण्डीव यूथाद् अपसे-धसे त्वं यो जेतुम् आशंससि धर्म-राजम् ॥ ) 3. 252. 5. J. Relationships with Himavant: (a) Daughters of Himavant: (i) Umā (हिमवतो गिरेर् दुहितरम् उमाम्) 12. 329. 49(1); (उमां … पितुर् दैन्यम् अनिच्छन्तीम्) 13. 127. 37; (ii) River Gaṅgā: (हिमवतः सुता) 3. 108. 8; 6. 114. 90; (शैलराजसुतां नदीम्) 3. 108. 4; (सुतावनीध्रस्य हरस्य भार्या) 13. 27. 88 (Nī. on Bom. Ed. 13. 26. 89: अवनीध्र-स्य मेरोः हिमवतो वा पर्वतस्य); (b) Sons of Himavant: (i) Mountain Krauñca (क्रौञ्चं हिमवतः सुतम्) 3. 214. 31; (ii) Mountain Arbuda (हिमवत्सुतम् अर्-बुदम्) 3. 80. 74; (c) Father-in-law of Śaṃkara (हिमवान् पुण्यः शंकरश्वशुरो गिरिः) 13. 26. 57; (d) General association: Gandhamādana mountain called हैमवत mountain 3. 157. 3. K. Bad omen: The falling down with great roar of thousands of summits of Kailāsa, Mandara and Himavant is mentioned among the bad omens noticed by Vyāsa before the war (तथा हिमवतो गिरेः सहस्रशो महाशब्दं शिखराणि पतन्ति च) 6. 3. 35. [See Śaiśira]
हिरण्यबिन्दु: Hiraṇyabindu m.: Name of a तीर्थ। A. Location: On the slope of the Himavant mountain (हिमवत्पार्श्वम्) 1. 207. 1. B. Holiness: According to the Tīrthavaṃśa narrated by Aṅgiras (13. 26. 3), if one who is controlled bathes in this तीर्थ (विक्षोभ्य) and bows down to the god-head lying in the Kuśa grass his sins are cleansed (हिरण्यबिन्दुं विक्षोभ्य प्रय-तश् चाभिवाद्य तम् । कुशेशयं च देव-त्वं पूयते तस्य किल्बिषम्) 13. 26. 10. C. Epic event: Arjuna, during the term of his exile, visited this तीर्थ; he bathed there and saw the best among the mountains (Himavant) and the sacred places (दृष्टवान् पर्वतश्रेष्ठं पुण्यान्य् आयतनानि च); he descended from there and went to the east 1. 207. 4-5; [For Hiraṇyabindu, as name of Agastyāśrama, see Section 1. 5A]
हिरण्यशृङ्ग: Hiraṇyaśṛṅga, Hiraṇyaśikhara, Hema-śṛṅga (1. 158. 17) m.: Name of a mountain. A. Location: Belongs to Himavant (हिमवतः … हेमशृङ्गात्) 1. 158. 17; to the north of Kailāsa, near the mountain Maināka (उत्तरेण तु कैलासं मैनाकं पर्वतं प्रति । हिरण्यशृङ्गः) 2. 3. 8; 6. 7. 40; on its slope is the lake Bindusaras (तस्य (i. e. हिरण्यशृङ्गस्य) पार्श्वे … बिन्दुसरो नाम) 6. 7. 41; 2. 3. 9. B. Description: Auspicious (भगवन्त्) 2. 3. 8; very big (सुमहन्त्) 6. 7. 40; heavenly (दिव्य) 6. 7. 40; full of jewels, full of large jewels (मणिमय) 6. 7. 40; (महामणि-मय) 2. 3. 8. C. Epic event: The Pāṇḍa-vas and Draupadī, when carried by Ghaṭo-tkaca to the place of Nara and Nārāyaṇa near the river Bhāgīrathī, saw from there Maināka, Hiraṇyaśikhara and Bindusaras 3. 145. 39. D. Past event: The divine Tripathagā (Gāṅgā), issuing from the world of Brahman, settled down at Hirṇyaśṛṅga and then was divided into seven streams (तत्र त्रिपथगा देवी प्रथमं तु प्रतिष्ठिता । ब्रह्मलोकाद् अपक्रान्ता सप्तधा प्रतिप-द्यते ॥ ) 6. 7. 44; formerly, Gaṅgā issued from Hemaśṛṅga of Himavant and on reach-ing the ocean got divided into seven streams (पुरा हिमवतश् चैषा हेमशृङ्गाद् विनिः-सृता । गङ्गा गत्वा समुद्राम्भः सप्त-धा प्रतिपद्यते) 1. 158. 17.
हिरण्यसरस्: Hiraṇyasaras nt.: Name of a तीर्थ। Located on the ocean in the west (पश्चि-मस्यां दिशि समुद्रे हिरण्यसरस् तीर्थम्) 12. 329. 46(5); since Soma was afflicted with consumption (यक्ष्मन्) he was advised by the sages to bathe in Hiraṇyasaras (आत्मा-नम् अभिषेचयस्व); Soma did accordingly and freed himself of the sin (गत्वा चात्मनः स्नपनम् अकरोत् । स्नात्वा चात्मानं पाप्मनो मोक्षयाम् आस) 12. 329. 46 (5-9); since Śoma got back his lustre there, the तीर्थ thereafter came to be known as Pra-bhāsa (तत्र चावभासितस् तीर्थे यदा सोमस् तदाप्रभृति तीर्थं तत् प्रभासम् इति नाम्ना ख्यातं बभूव) 12. 329. 46(10). [See Prabhāsa]
हिरण्वती: Hiraṇvatī f.: Name of a river. A. Location: Listed by Saṃjaya among the rivers of the Bhāratavarṣa; people used its water for drinking 6. 10. 24, 13; in Kurukṣetra (कुरुक्षेत्रे … नद्यास् तीरे हिरण्वत्याः) 1. 95. 8; (सरितं … कुरु-क्षेत्रे हिरण्वतीम्) 5. 149. 73; B. Descrip-tion: Holy (पुण्या), having bright water (शुचिजला); free from pebbles and mud (शर्-करापङ्कवर्जिता), having easy fords (सूप-तीर्था) (Nī., however, on Bom. Ed. 5. 152. 7: सूपतीर्थां शोभनोपकण्ठाम्) 5. 149. 73; all the rivers listed by Saṃjaya are said to be mothers of the universe and very strong 6. 10. 35 (for citation see Atikṛṣṇā). C. Epic events: (1) Citrāṅgada, son of Śaṃtanu, and his namesake, the king of the Gandharvas (गन्धर्वराजो बलवांस् तुल्य-नामा 1. 95. 7), fought a battle lasting for three years (समास् तिस्रो ऽभवद् रणः) on the bank of Hiraṇvatī; in this battle the former was killed 1. 95. 8-10; (2) The camp of the Pāṇḍavas was laid by Dhṛṣṭa-dyumna near the river Hiraṇvatī (शिबिरं मापयाम् आस धृष्टद्युम्नः … आसाद्य सरितं … हिरण्वतीम्) 5. 149. 72-73; when the Pāṇḍavas were encamped there Duryo-dhana sent Ulūka as his messenger to them (हिरण्वत्यां णिविष्टेषु पाण्डवेषु) 5. 157. 1. D. Importance: Finds mention in the Daivata-Ṛṣi-Vaṃśa 13. 151. 20.
हेमकूट: Hemakūṭa m.: Name of a mountain. (also called Ṛṣabhakūṭa 3. 109. 7; once identified with Kailāsa 6. 7. 39). A. Location: Listed by Saṃjaya among the six mountains which stretch towards the east and merge at both ends in the eastern and the western oceans (प्रागायता महाराज षद् एते रत्नपर्वताः । अवगाढा ह्य् उभ-यतः समुद्रौ पूर्वपश्चिमौ) 6. 7. 2; the distance between them is thousands of योजनस् (तेषाम् अन्तरविष्कम्भो योजनानि सहस्रशः) 6. 7. 4; it lies between Haima-vatavarṣa and Harivarṣa; the Varṣa beyond Hemakūṭa is Harivarṣa (इदं तु भारतं वर्षं ततो हैमवतं परम् । हेमकूटात् परं चैव हरिवर्षं प्रचक्षते) 6. 7. 6; identified with Kailāsa (हेमकूटस् तु सुमहान् कैलासो नाम पर्वतः) 6. 7. 39; to the north of Kailāsa and towards Maināka is the Hiraṇyaśṛṅga mountain 6. 7. 40; near the rivers Nandā and Aparanandā (ततः प्रयातः … नन्दाम् अपरनन्दां च नद्यौ … । स पर्वतं समासाद्य हेमकूटम्) 3. 109. 1-2; 3. 109. 18-19. B. Description: Free from disease (अना-मय) 3. 109. 2; big (महागिरि) 3. 109. 14; (सुमहन्त्) 6. 7. 39; all the six mountains listed by Saṃjaya are full of jewels (रत्न-पर्वताः) 6. 7. 2 and resorted to by Siddhas and Cāraṇas (सिद्धचारणसेविताः) 6. 7. 4. C. Characteristics: (1) Many unthinkable wonders happen on the mountain (अचिन्त्यान् अद्भुतान् भावान् ददर्श सुबहून् नृपः); spoken words turn into clouds and rocks by thousands and hence people cannot climb it (वाचो यत्राभवन् मेघा उपलाश् च सहस्र-शः । नाशक्नुवंस् तम् आरोढुम् … जनाः ॥ ) 3. 109. 3; wind always blows there and it rains continuously; the oblation bearing god (Fire) can be seen there morning and evening (वायुर् नित्यं ववौ यत्र नित्यं देवश् च वर्षति । सायं प्रातश् च भग-वान् दृश्यते हव्यवाहनः ॥ ) 3. 109. 4; (2) One cannot even look at this mountain, let alone climb it; one who has not practised austerities cannot look at it or climb it (नाशक्नुवन्न् अभिद्रष्टुं कुत एवाधिरो-हितुम् ॥ नातप्ततपसा शक्यो द्रष्टुम् एष महागिरिः । आरोढुं वापि कौन्तेय) 3. 109. 13-14; (3) Guhyakas live there (हेम-कूटे तु गुह्यकाः) 6. 7. 48; King Vaiśra-vaṇa, along with the Guhyakas, enjoys him-self there (यत्र वैश्रवणो राजा गुह्य-कैः सह मोदते) 6. 7. 39. D. Epic event: Yudhiṣṭhira having reached Hemakūṭa saw many wonders there 3. 109. 5; Lomaśa gave to him the explanation of these wonders 3. 109. 6-17 (see the next section); he advised Yudhiṣṭhira to bathe in the river Nandā flowing along the mountain since a bath destroyed the sin instantly 3. 109. 18; he also asked him to restrain his speech (नियतवाग् भव) 3. 109. 14. E. Past events: (1) An ascetic named Ṛṣabha once lived on this mountain (hence called Ṛṣabhakūṭa ?) and was practising austerities for many hundred years (अनेकशतवर्षायुस् तपस्वी); he got angry when he was drawn into conversation by others; so he told the mountain to release rocks if any one uttered a word there; he summoned wind and bade him not to make noise; hence if any one tried to speak there he was restrained by a cloud (स वै संभाष्यमाणो ऽन्यैः कोपाद् गिरिम् उवाच ह । य इह व्याहरेत् कश्चिद् उपलान् उत्सृजेस् तदा ॥ वातं चाहूय मा शब्दम् इत्य् उवाच स तापसः । व्याहरंश् चैव पुरुषो मेघेन विनिवार्यते ॥ ) 3. 109. 7-9; (2) When gods formerly came to the river Nandā (flowing near Hemakūṭa) men followed there to see the gods; since the gods, Indra and the rest, did not wish to be seen by men they made the land inaccessible making this mountain an obstacle (दुर्गं चक्रुर् इमं देशं गिरिप्रत्यूहरूपकम्); hence men cannot even look at the mountain, let alone climb it; the gods then always per-formed best sacrifices there; the signs of those sacrifices could even now be seen in the form of the sprawling दूर्वा grass having the form of sacrificial grass (कुश) and many trees having the shape of sacrificial posts (यूप) (तेषाम् एतानि लिङ्गानि दृश्यन्ते ऽद्यापि भारत ॥ कुशाकारेव दुर्वेयं … यूप-प्रकारा बहवो वृक्षाश् चेमे ॥ ) 3. 109. 11-16; (3) Hamakūṭa was one of the mountains seen by Mārkaṇḍeya in the belly of the Bāla (3. 186. 83 = Nārāyaṇa 3. 187. 3) 3. 186. 101. हैरण्वती: Hairaṇvatī f.: Name of a river. The river flows in the Hairaṇvatavarṣa 6. 9. 5.

Founding and explanation of the name: The city was founded by king Hastin, the son of Suhotra and Suvarṇā; that is why the city is called Hāstinapura (तस्याम् (i. e. सुवर्णायाम्) अस्य (i. e. सुहोत्रस्य) जज्ञे हस्ती । य इदं हास्तिन-पुरं मापयाम् आस । एतद् अस्य हास्तिन-पुरत्वम्) 1. 90. 36; B. Description: Delightful (रम्य) 1. 94. 10; the best city (नगरोत्तम) 13. 153. 5; praised as the best among towns (ततो निर्वचनं लोके सर्वराष्ट्रेष्व् अवर्तत ॥ … पुराणां गजसाह्वयम् ॥ ) 1. 102. 21-22 (Nī. on Bom. Ed. 1. 109. 23: निर्वचनं प्रशंसा); comparable with the city of Indra (पुरन्-दरपुरोपम) 1. 94. 38; the houses in Hāstinapura looked like white mountains (श्वेतपर्वतरूपेभ्यो गृहेभ्यः) 11. 9. 9; the capital town of the Kurus (कुरूणाम् पुटभेदने) 1. 94. 10 (Nī. on Bom. Ed. 1. 100. 12: पुटभेदने पत्तने). C. Des-cription of the town on specific occasions: (1) On the arrival of Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna: full of delighted people (संप्रहृष्टनरा-कुल) 14. 51. 24; (2) When the still-born child, Parīkṣit, was brought back to life: people decorated the town with heaps of garlands; citizens beautified their houses with small and big flags; the highways were decorated with flowers; the city looked bright and produced sound similar to the tide of the ocean; owing to the sound of dancing and singing of dancers the town appeared like the residence of Vaiśravaṇa (Kubera); the city's empty places were filled with bards in thousands, accom-panied by women; flags moving in the blow-ing wind as if pointed out to the Kurus the northern and the southern direction; the high-placed king's officer then announc-ed to the people enjoyment, all through the night, in which ornaments of jewels were to be displayed (अलंचक्रुश् च माल्यौ-घैः पुरुषा नागसाह्वयम् ॥ पताकाभिर् विचित्राभिर् ध्वजैश् च विविधैर् अपि । वेश्मानि समलंचक्रुः पौराश् चापि जनाधिप ॥ राजमार्गाश् च तत्रासन् सुमनोभिर् अलं-कृताः । शुशुभे तत् पुरं चापि समुद्रौ-घनिभस्वनम् ॥ नर्तकैश् चापि नृत्यद्-भिर् गायकानां च निस्वनैः । आसीद् वैश्रवणस्येव निवासस् तत् पुरं तदा ॥ बन्दिभिश् च नरै राजन् स्त्री सहायैः सह-स्रशः । तत्र तत्र विविक्तेषु समन्ताद् उपशोभितम् ॥ पताका धूयमानाश् च श्व-सता मातरिश्वना । अदर्शयन्न् इव तदा कुरून् वै दक्षिणोत्तरान् ॥ अघोषयत् तदा चापि पुरुषो राजधूर्गतः । सर्वरात्रिविहारो ऽद्य रत्नाभरणलक्षणः ॥ ) 14. 69. 13-20; (3) After the departure of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Gāndhārī, Kuntī and Vidura, the whole town with its old men, women and child-ren became cheerless, the town was as if without any sound as at the end of a festival (तद् अहृष्टम् इवाकूजं गतोत्सवम् इवाभ-वत् । नगरं हास्तिनपुरं सस्त्रीवृद्ध-कुमारकं ॥ ) 15. 24. 14. D. Epic events: The name of the city occurs in connection with many important events; on various occasions, however, Hāstinapura is referred to simply by words such as नगर or पुर (in the following listing references of this type where the city is not directly named are likely to be incomplete) (1) Jana-mejaya, son of Parikṣit, after the comple-tion of his सत्र at Kurukṣetra, returned to Hāstinapura and searched for a suita-ble Purohita who could pacify the evil act done by him (स तस्मिन् सत्रे समाप्ते हास्तिनपुरं प्रत्येत्य पुरोहितम् अनुरू-पम् अन्विच्छमानः परं यत्नम् अकरोद् यो मे पापकृत्यां शमयेद् इति) 1. 3. 10 (Nī. on Bom. Ed. 1. 3. 11: पापकृत्यां शापरू-पां बलायुःप्राणनिकृन्तनीं देवताम्); (2) Uttaṅka, wanting to take revenge on Takṣaka for his misdeed, started for Hāsti-napura; (उत्तङ्कः … हास्तिनपुरं प्रतस्-थे । स हास्तिनपुरं प्राप्य) 1. 3. 177-178; (3) Parikṣit, after placing the body of a dead snake on the shoulder of Śṛṅgin's father returned to his town Gajāhvaya (स्वनगरं प्रतियातो गजाह्वयम्) 1. 37. 9; (4) When Kāśyapa ceased from pro-ceeding to Hāstinapura, Takṣaka himself went speedily to the town Nāgasāhvaya (निवृत्ते काश्यपे … । जगाम तक्षकस् तूर्-णं नगरं नागसाह्वयम् ॥ ) 1. 39. 20; (5) Śaṃtanu ruled the earth from Hāsti-napura, the capital town of the Kurus (स हास्तिनपुरे रम्ये कुरूणां पुटभेदने । वसन् … अन्वशाद् वै वसुंधराम्) 1. 94. 10; (6) Śaṃtanu, unwilling to agree to the condition laid down by the Dāśa, re-turned to Hāstinapura (प्रत्ययाद् धास्तिन-पुरम्) 1. 94. 53; (7) Bhīṣma took Satya-vatī on a chariot to Hāstinapura and repor-ted to Śaṃtanu (आगम्य हास्तिनपुरम् शंतनोः संन्यवेदयत्) 1. 94. 92; (8) Bhīṣma having won the Kāśi princesses, brought them to Hāstinapura (प्रययौ हास्तिनपुरम्) 1. 96. 41; (9) Kings who formerly collected wealth from Kuru kings (wealth described in 1. 105. 16-18) were made to pay it back as tribute by Pāṇḍu, king of Nāgapura and the lion of Nāgapura (तत् सर्वं प्रतिजग्राह राजा नागपुरा-धिपः) 1. 105. 18; (ते नागपुरसिंहेन पाण्डुना करदाः कृताः) 1. 105. 21; he then returned to Gajasāhvaya (ययौ पाण्डुः … पुरं च गजसाह्वयम्) 1. 105. 19; Bhīṣma and others who lived in Nāgapura (नाग-पुरालयाः) went out (of the town) a little distance to receive Pāṇḍu 1. 105. 23; his large army, feeling pain due to the burden of wealth, also started for the town (सा पुराभिमुखी राजन् जगाम महती चमूः । कृच्छ्राद् द्रविणभारार्ता) 14. 64. 20; (70) Kṛṣṇa along with the Vṛṣṇis, came to the town Vāraṇasāhvaya for the horse sacrifice of Yudhiṣṭhira (पुरं वार-णसाह्वयम्) 14. 65. 1; for the reception of the Vṛṣṇi heroes, (king's) officers decorated Nāgasāhvaya with heaps of garlands and with various variegated, small and big flags; the citizens decorated also their houses (अलंचक्रुश् च … पुरुषा नागसाह्वयम् । वेश्मानि समलंचक्रुः पौराश् चापि) 14. 69. 13-14; the highways were decorated with flowers and the town, filled with the noise similar to that of the flood of the ocean, shone (शुशुभे तत् पुरं चापि समुद्र-उघनिभस्वनम्) 14. 69. 16; dancing and singing, filled the town; the city was adorn-ed by bards in thousands together with their women; flags, moved by wind, as if showed the southern and northern direc-tions to the Kurus; a highly placed king's officer announced merry-making all through the night, displaying ornaments of jewels (पताका धूयमानाश् च श्वसता मातरिश्व-ना । अदर्शयन्न् इव तदा कुरून् वै दक्षिणो-त्तरान् ॥ अघोषयत् तदा चापि पुरुषः राज-धूर्गतः । सर्वरात्रिविहारो ऽद्य रत्नाभ-रणलक्षणः) 14. 69. 17-20; the Pāṇḍavas who received the Vṛṣṇis, entered with them the town Vāraṇasāhvaya (पुरं वारण-साह्वयम्) 14. 70. 2; the Pāṇḍavas, with their friends and ministers, entered their own town placing the treasure in front of them (ते कोशम् अग्रतः कृत्वा विविशुः स्व-पुरं तदा) 14. 70. 4; (71) Some days later, Vyāsa also arrived at the town Nāga-sāhvaya (नगरं नागसाह्वयम्) 14. 70. 10; (72) When Arjuna was to leave the town to accompany the horse of the Aśva-medha, the whole town including children gathered to see him (आकुमारं तदा राजन्न् आगमद् तत् पुरं विभो) 14. 72. 9; Aśvamedha horse, after wandering over the earth as far as the ocean, turned back and faced the direction of the town Nāgāhvaya (स तु वाजी समुद्रान्तां पर्-येत्य पृथिवीम् इमाम् ॥ निवृत्तो ऽभिमुखो राजन् येन नागाह्वयं पुरम्) 14. 83. 1; (73) The horse, after Arjuna's battle with Śakuni's son in the Gāndhāra country, returned to the direction of the town Nāgā-hvaya (न्यवर्तत ततो वाजी येन नागाह्व-यं पुरम्) 14. 86. 1; (7) Dhṛtarāṣṭra, before leaving for forest life, advised Yudhi-ṣṭhira to look after the safety of the town (Hāstinapura); he asked him to see that it was well protected by strong ramparts and arched doorways; it should have on all sides high watchtowers, close to each other with enough space for six persons to walk; it should have sufficient entrances, large in size; they should be well distributed and protected by mechanical devices (पुरं च ते सुगुप्तं स्याद् दृढप्राकारतोरणम् । अट्टाट्टालकसंबाधं षट्पथं सर्वतो-दिशम् ॥ तस्य द्वाराणि कार्याणि पर्याप्तानि बृहन्ति च । सर्वतः सुविभक्तानि यन्त्रैर् आरक्षितानि च ॥ ) 15. 9. 16-17) (Nī. on Bom. Ed. 15. 5. 16: अट्टाः दुर्गोपरिभागे सञ्चार-स्थानानि, षट्पदं (this is Nī.'s reading) षड्भिः पदैः पदनीयैः स्थानैर् युक्तं तेन सप्तप्राकारम् इति गम्यते । तत्र सप्तमस्यान्तःपुरत्वात् षड् एवान्येषां पदनीयानि स्थानानि); (75) At the time of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's departure, the citizens of Gajāhvaya were very much grieved (दुः-खितः पौरवर्गो गजाह्वये ऽतीव बभूव) 15. 21. 12; he went out of Gajasāhvaya through the gate called Vardhamāna (स वर्धमानद्वारेण निर्ययौ गजसाह्वयात्) 15. 22. 3; (76) Yudhiṣṭhira requested Kuntī not to follow Dhṛtarāṣṭra to the forest but to return to the town and be with her daughters-in-law (वधूपरिवृता राज्ञि नगरं गन्तुम् अर्हसि) 15. 22. 8; (77) After the departure of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Pāṇḍavas, along with women, returned to the town (पाण्डवाः … स्त्रीसहिताः सर्वे पुरं प्रविविशुस् तदा); the whole town Hāstinapura, with its women, old men and children, then became cheerless, noiseless, as after a festival (नगरं हास्तिन्पुरं तद् अहृष्टम् इवाकूजं गतोत्सवम् इवाभवत् सस्त्रीवृद्धकुमारकम् । ) 15. 24. 13-14; (78) When Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the forest was surrounded by Yudhiṣṭhira and others, as well as by citizens, he felt he was as though in Gajasāhvaya as before (मेने … पुरेव गजसाह्वये) 15. 31. 18; (रमे चाहं  … पुरेव गजसाह्वये) 15. 44. 15; (79) When permitted by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Gāndhārī and Kuntī, Yudhiṣṭhira returned to the town Hāstinapura (नगरं हास्तिनपुरं पुनर् आयात्) 15. 44. 52; (80) When Yudhi-ṣṭhira heard about the death of Dhṛta-rāṣṭra, Gāndhārī and Kuntī, he went out (of the town) to the river Gaṅgā (निर्ययौ सह सोदर्यैः सदारः … गङ्गां प्रजग्-मुः) 15. 47. 10-11; after offering water libations to the dead (15. 47. 12), Yudhi-ṣṭhira and others returned to town but stayed outside it until they were freed from impurity (शौचं निवर्तयन्तस् ते तत्रोषुर् नगराद् बहिः) 15. 47. 13; on the twelfth day he performed the श्राद्ध and gave gifts (15. 47. 16) and then entered the town Vāraṇāhvaya (प्रविवेषा … नगरं वारणा-ह्वयम्) 15. 47. 21; Dhṛtarāṣṭra had lived a total of fifteen years in the town (Hāstina-pura) after the death of his sons in the battle, and three years in the forest (एवं वर्षाण्य् अतीतानि धृतराष्ट्रस्य धीमतः । वनवासे तदा त्रीणि नगरे दश पञ्च च ॥ हतपुत्रस्य संग्रामे) 15. 47. 25-26; (81) Consoled by Vyāsa over the death of Kṛṣṇa and others, Arjuna returned to the town Nāgasāhvaya (ययौ पार्थो नग-रं नागसाह्वयम्) 16. 9. 37; (82) When Yudhiṣṭhira decided to start on the great journey (महाप्रस्थान) he gave the king-dom of Hāstinapura to Parikṣit and of Śakraprastha to Vajra (परिक्षिद् धास्तिन-पुरे शक्रप्रस्थे तु यादवः) 17. 1. 9; he, along with his brothers, Draupadī and a dog, left Gajasāhvaya on their great journey; he was followed by the citizens and the women of the inner apartments; all the citizens then returned to (the town) (निर्य-यौ गजसाह्वयात् … न्यवर्तन्त ततः सर्वे नरा नगरवासिनः) 17. 1. 23-24; (83) After completing his सर्पसत्र, king Jana-mejaya took leave of the officiating priests and came back from Takṣaśilā to Gajāhvaya (ततः तक्षशिलायाः स पुनर् आयाद् गजाह्-वयम्) 18. 5. 29. E. Past event: When Kaṇva asked his pupils to take Śakuntalā and her son to her husband Duḥṣanta, (1. 68. 10), they all left for Gajasāhvaya (ते सर्वे … प्रातिष्ठन्त … गजसाह्वयम्) 1. 68. 12. F. Simile: (1) With the dances of the dancers and sounds of the songs, the town (Hāstinapura) became like the resi-dence of Kubera (नर्तकैश् चापि नृत्यद्-भिर् गायनानां च निस्वनैः । आसीद् वैश्र-वणस्येव निवासस् तत् पुरं तदा ॥ ) 14. 69. 17.
